title: People are health
hookLine: a 2010 review linked strong social ties to longer life (Holt-Lunstad et al.)
last: WHAT WOULD I SAY TO A FRIEND.

cards: Stop smoking. Move more. Eat your vegetables.
Sleep. That's the familiar list. Here's advice that rarely makes it on: call your sister.
Have dinner with your neighbors. Keep the friend who makes you laugh. It sounds like greeting-card stuff, the soft extra you get to once the real health work is done.

In 2010 a team of researchers gathered nearly a hundred and fifty studies, following hundreds of thousands of people for years, and asked a hard question: do people with stronger relationships actually live longer?

teach.b: Julianne Holt-Lunstad and her colleagues combined 148 studies with more than three hundred thousand people, followed for about seven and a half years on average.
People with stronger social relationships were about fifty percent more likely to be alive at the end of the studies than people with weaker ones.
The authors noted that the size of that link was comparable to well-known risks like smoking. Now, remember: compared to what? These were mostly observational studies.
Healthy people may find it easier to keep friends, and many things travel together.
The researchers tried to adjust for age, health and other factors, and the link held, but a review like this shows a strong association, not proof that a phone call adds a year.
Still, the authors argued that a link this size means social ties deserve the same attention as other health risks. Then the old voices, each in its own house.
Ecclesiastes in the Hebrew Bible says two are better than one, because if one falls, the other can lift him up.
The Stoic Seneca wrote letters to his friend Lucilius about what a true friend is, and why even a wise person wants one.

teach.h: YOUR FRIEND IS YOUR NEEDS ANSWERED.
teach.b: And Kahlil Gibran, in The Prophet, put it in one line: "Your friend is your needs answered." This caps a week: Brewer. Sixty-six days.
The cue does the remembering. Start with small things. Silently wish them well.
What would I say to a friend.
And now, other people. Those habits may come easier, and kinder, with company. Company isn't the reward after the health work.

how: Public-health researchers now treat social connection as a health factor, and several traditions build practice around community, from shared meals to weekly gatherings; people on their own paths often keep a regular call or meal with friends.

games.q: you've been meaning to call an old friend for months. it feels awkward now. what does this week suggest?
o: send two real lines today, after your cue.
games.why: easy beats heroic: a small message today beats a perfect call someday. people are health.

practice: Let the faces of people you haven't talked to in a while pass by, one at a time, without guilt: a friend who drifted, a cousin, an old neighbor. Pick one, picture them answering the phone, and hear their voice.
Rest with that face in mind.

wordCard.voice: Holt-Lunstad, whose review linked strong social ties to a longer life, comparable, the authors said, to risks like smoking.

carryVoice: Your line: two are better than one. Not a like, not a heart: a voice, or at least a real message. That's day three hundred fifteen.
